bib.title: Full Parameter Fine-tuning for Large Language Models with Limited Resources
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv:2306.09782v2, 6 Jun 2024; the PDF does not print a venue)

question: Can all parameters of a large language model be fine-tuned with very limited GPU memory?
hypothesis: Plain SGD is an acceptable optimizer for fine-tuning LLMs because their loss surface is smooth, so optimizer states and stored gradient tensors can be removed.
contributions: A theoretical analysis suggesting that SGD can successfully fine-tune the full parameters of LLMs.
LOMO (LOw-Memory Optimization), which fuses gradient computation and parameter update to save GPU memory without harming fine-tuning.
An evaluation of memory usage and throughput, supported by downstream results on SuperGLUE.

method.summary: LOMO uses plain SGD and updates each parameter as soon as its gradient is computed during backpropagation (via hooks), so at most one parameter's gradient is held and no optimizer state exists. Stability is handled with value clipping or an extra backward pass for the gradient norm, dynamic loss scaling, and full-precision arithmetic for some operations. Evaluated on LLaMA 7B to 65B for memory, throughput and SuperGLUE accuracy against zero-shot and LoRA.
method.task: full-parameter fine-tuning of LLMs under a memory budget; SuperGLUE classification with 1,000 training examples

datasets.preprocessing: Prompts are the same as MeZO; at inference each label or candidate is inserted into the prompt and the label with the highest average log-likelihood is chosen

models.name: LLaMA with LoRA
models.architecture: LoRA on q and v projections

training.optimizer: LOMO (fused SGD); AdamW for the LoRA baseline
training.warmup: ratio: LOMO {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}; LoRA 0.05; LoRA+LOMO LOMO part 0.05, 0.1

training.precision: mixed precision (FP16) with dynamic loss scaling; gradient and parameter converted to full precision for normalisation and scaling
training.regularisation: Max grad norm 1.0 (Table 4); value clipping suggested for learning rates below 1e-3
training.hardware: server with 8 x RTX 3090 (24GB), PCIe interconnect; parameter partitioning with ZeRO-3
training.compute: 65B on 1000 samples of 512 tokens: about 3.6 hours on 8 x RTX 3090
training.seeds: one random seed; the best result is reported

other.LoRA config: rq = rv = 2, alpha 16 (LoRA+LOMO: rq = rv in {1, 2, 4, 8}, alpha 16)
other.loss scaling: scale factor doubled if no overflow in a specified number of backward passes, halved and step dropped otherwise (the number of passes is not stated)
other.backward passes: two backward passes when gradient normalisation or loss-scale overflow detection is needed (one to check, one to update)

inference.decoding: no generation: score each candidate label by average log-likelihood in the prompt and pick the highest
inference.samples: one run with one random seed; best result reported

limits: Gradient normalisation needs an additional backward pass in the current implementation, which slows training.
Experiments cover only a subset of SuperGLUE; throughput was not evaluated on A100 or other advanced GPUs.
Downstream results use 1,000 training examples, one random seed, and the best result is reported; no variance or significance test.
Only SGD is used; the authors say there is no guarantee that SGD is as powerful as modern optimizers, and the smooth-loss argument holds only for tasks close to pre-training.
Exact immediate update is not possible with current PyTorch hooks; at most one parameter's gradient is held in memory.
Value clipping performs worse at high learning rates; grouped gradient-norm approximation is biased and is called controversial.
Authors attribute cases where LOMO loses to LoRA to the small training set and different architectures, without testing it.
Memory is now mostly parameters; the authors list quantisation as future work.
